claim: STN neurons were driven to spike with intracellular current pulses at frequencies ranging from 10 to 200 Hz in 1 min epochs, which evoked rhythmic spiking at these frequencies.
source: Neurons were driven to spike with intracellular current pulses at frequencies ranging from 10 to 200 Hz in 1 min epochs, which evoked rhythmic spiking at these frequencies (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: The manuscript describes ex vivo experimental data showing that current pulses evoked rhythmic spiking in STN neurons.

claim: Calcium, as measured by changes in GCaMP6s fluorescence, increased during firing at 10–200 Hz.
source: Calcium, as measured by changes in GCaMP6s fluorescence, similarly increased during firing at 10–200 Hz (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data from combined electrophysiology and calcium imaging showing that GCaMP6s fluorescence increased with firing.

claim: STN neurons showed rhythmic spiking that matched the frequency of pulsatile stimulation.
source: Again, STN neurons showed rhythmic spiking that matched the frequency of pulsatile stimulation (Figure 1E, insets), and calcium signals correlated with firing rates up to about 100 Hz, and were variable between 100 and 200 Hz (Figure 1G, inset).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that STN neurons fired rhythmically in response to pulsatile stimulation.

claim: Calcium signals correlated with firing rates up to about 100 Hz, and were variable between 100 and 200 Hz.
source: Again, STN neurons showed rhythmic spiking that matched the frequency of pulsatile stimulation (Figure 1E, insets), and calcium signals correlated with firing rates up to about 100 Hz, and were variable between 100 and 200 Hz (Figure 1G, inset).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing the relationship between calcium signals and firing rates at different frequencies.

claim: Some groups have speculated that high-frequency DBS may cause some neurons to enter depolarization block.
source: As some groups have speculated that high-frequency DBS may cause some neurons to enter depolarization block, we also tested the firing and calcium signals associated with constant current ('square wave') stimulation.
evidence: The manuscript references speculation from other groups about depolarization block during high-frequency DBS.

claim: During constant current stimulation, STN neurons fired only transiently, appearing to enter depolarization block.
source: During such stimulation, STN neurons fired only transiently, appearing to enter depolarization block (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that STN neurons fired transiently during constant current stimulation.

claim: Under conditions of forced depolarization block, evoked calcium signals fell between those associated with 10 and 50–60 Hz spiking.
source: Under these circumstances, evoked calcium signals fell between those associated with 10 and 50–60 Hz spiking (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing calcium signal levels during depolarization block.

claim: The relationship between spiking and GCaMP calcium signals may break down at very high firing frequencies, or under conditions of forced depolarization block.
source: These experiments suggest that the relationship between spiking and GCaMP calcium signals may break down at very high firing frequencies, or under conditions of forced depolarization block.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference from the experimental data about the limitations of GCaMP signals.

claim: At more moderate firing frequencies, GCaMP calcium signals correlate with STN firing.
source: However, at more moderate firing frequencies, GCaMP calcium signals correlate with STN firing.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the experimental data about the correlation between GCaMP signals and firing at moderate frequencies.

claim: 6-OHDA-treated mice showed both decreased movement velocity (1.3±0.1 cm/s parkinsonian vs. 3.1±0.4 cm/s healthy, p=8.23 × 10–5) and an ipsilesional rotational bias (p=1.40 × 10–3) when compared to healthy mice.
source: As observed in prior studies (Bové and Perier, 2012; Campos et al., 2013; Carvalho et al., 2013; Ungerstedt, 1968), 6-OHDA-treated mice showed both decreased movement velocity (1.3±0.1 cm/s parkinsonian vs. 3.1±0.4 cm/s healthy, p=8.23 × 10–5) and an ipsilesional rotational bias (p=1.40 × 10–3) when compared to healthy mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing behavioral deficits in 6-OHDA-treated mice, supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Movement velocity and rotation bias did not differ significantly between parkinsonian mice with and without STN implants.
source: Additionally, movement velocity and rotation bias did not differ significantly between parkinsonian mice with and without STN implants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, p=0.66 for velocity, p=0.97 for rotation), suggesting that local, implant-related STN tissue disturbance did not alter gross movement parameters.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data comparing behavioral parameters in parkinsonian mice with and without implants.

claim: Local, implant-related STN tissue disturbance did not alter gross movement parameters.
source: Additionally, movement velocity and rotation bias did not differ significantly between parkinsonian mice with and without STN implants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, p=0.66 for velocity, p=0.97 for rotation), suggesting that local, implant-related STN tissue disturbance did not alter gross movement parameters.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference from the experimental data about the lack of effect of implants on movement.

claim: STN single units showed baseline firing rates of approximately 5–10 spikes/s.
source: STN single units showed baseline firing rates of approximately 5–10 spikes/s (Figure 1K), well within the linear range for GCaMP6s (Figure 1G, inset).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing baseline firing rates of STN neurons.

claim: STN single unit baseline firing rates are well within the linear range for GCaMP6s.
source: STN single units showed baseline firing rates of approximately 5–10 spikes/s (Figure 1K), well within the linear range for GCaMP6s (Figure 1G, inset).
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference from the experimental data about the suitability of GCaMP6s for measuring STN activity.

claim: The firing of STN units showed a marked change in firing rate around movement onset, increasing just prior to, and peaking just following movement initiation (approximately 1 spike/s over the baseline rate).
source: The firing of STN units showed a marked change in firing rate around movement onset, increasing just prior to, and peaking just following movement initiation (approximately 1 spike/s over the baseline rate).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing changes in STN firing rate around movement onset.

claim: Population calcium signals showed a similar increase around movement onset, but lagged the rise in single-unit firing rate by ~1 s, likely due to the slower kinetics of GCaMP6s.
source: Population calcium signals showed a similar increase around movement onset, but lagged the rise in single-unit firing rate by ~1 s, likely due to the slower kinetics of GCaMP6s (Markowitz et al., 2018; Figure 1L).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing calcium signals around movement onset and cites a reference about GCaMP6s kinetics.

claim: In healthy animals, STN GCaMP signals increased around movement onset.
source: As in parkinsonian mice, we found that in healthy animals, STN GCaMP signals increased around movement onset (Figure 1M).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing STN calcium signals in healthy mice around movement onset.

claim: STN calcium signals and electrophysiology appear to capture a slightly time-shifted, but qualitatively similar increase in activity when aligned to behavior.
source: Thus, STN calcium signals and electrophysiology appear to capture a slightly time-shifted, but qualitatively similar increase in activity when aligned to behavior.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference from the experimental data comparing calcium signals and electrophysiology.

claim: There is a correlation between spiking and GCaMP6s signal.
source: Together, these ex vivo and in vivo experiments show a correlation between spiking and GCaMP6s signal, and therefore support the utility of fiber photometry as a proxy for neuronal activity in the context of STN DBS.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the experimental data about the correlation between spiking and GCaMP6s signal.

claim: Fiber photometry is a useful proxy for neuronal activity in the context of STN DBS.
source: Together, these ex vivo and in vivo experiments show a correlation between spiking and GCaMP6s signal, and therefore support the utility of fiber photometry as a proxy for neuronal activity in the context of STN DBS.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the experimental data about the utility of fiber photometry.

claim: The direct impact of STN DBS on STN neural activity remains unclear: some studies indicate that STN DBS decreases STN firing rates, while recordings in downstream nuclei indicate STN activity may increase.
source: The direct impact of STN DBS on STN neural activity remains unclear: some studies indicate that STN DBS decreases STN firing rates, while recordings in downstream nuclei indicate STN activity may increase.
evidence: The manuscript references conflicting findings from prior studies about the effect of STN DBS on STN activity.

claim: Many different parameter sets were effective for STN DBS, across a broad frequency range.
source: Consistent with our previous findings in the same mouse model (Schor and Nelson, 2019), many different parameter sets were effective, across a broad frequency range.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data and cites a previous study showing that multiple DBS parameter sets were effective.

claim: Average movement velocity was increased by low- (5–40 Hz), medium- (60–100 Hz), and high-frequency (120–180 Hz) STN DBS.
source: Grouping these parameter sets by stimulation frequency, we found that average movement velocity was increased by low- (5–40 Hz), medium- (60–100 Hz), and high-frequency (120–180 Hz) STN DBS (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that STN DBS at various frequencies increased movement velocity.

claim: 60–100 and 120–180 Hz DBS produced similar benefits in movement velocity.
source: We found that 60–100 and 120–180 Hz DBS produced similar benefits in movement velocity, so focused on 60 and 100 Hz stimulation for subsequent analyses; 60 or 100 Hz stimulation improved multiple movement metrics (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-K).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing similar benefits of different DBS frequencies.

claim: At 60 Hz stimulation, STN DBS increased movement velocity (p=3.92 × 10–9) and percent time moving (p=3.53 × 10–9), while not significantly altering rotation bias (p=0.71) or causing prolonged dyskinesias.
source: At either 60 or 100 Hz stimulation, STN DBS increased movement velocity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C,G,H; p=3.92 × 10–9 for 60 Hz, p=5.53 × 10–8 for 100 Hz) and percent time moving (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,I; p=3.53 × 10–9 for 60 Hz, p=1.46 × 10–8 for 100 Hz), while not significantly altering rotation bias (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,J; p=0.71 for 60 Hz, p=0.47 for 100 Hz) or causing prolonged dyskinesias (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F,K).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing the effects of 60 Hz STN DBS on multiple behavioral measures.

claim: At 100 Hz stimulation, STN DBS increased movement velocity (p=5.53 × 10–8) and percent time moving (p=1.46 × 10–8), while not significantly altering rotation bias (p=0.47) or causing prolonged dyskinesias.
source: At either 60 or 100 Hz stimulation, STN DBS increased movement velocity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C,G,H; p=3.92 × 10–9 for 60 Hz, p=5.53 × 10–8 for 100 Hz) and percent time moving (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,I; p=3.53 × 10–9 for 60 Hz, p=1.46 × 10–8 for 100 Hz), while not significantly altering rotation bias (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,J; p=0.71 for 60 Hz, p=0.47 for 100 Hz) or causing prolonged dyskinesias (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F,K).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing the effects of 100 Hz STN DBS on multiple behavioral measures.

claim: STN DBS at 60 Hz caused a significant increase in STN calcium signals (p=1.19 × 10–7) in parallel with its impact on movement velocity (p=7.11 × 10–9).
source: Surprisingly, in parallel with its impact on movement velocity (p=7.11 × 10–9), STN DBS at 60 Hz caused a significant increase in STN calcium signals (Figure 2C–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B; p=1.19 × 10–7).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that 60 Hz STN DBS increased both movement velocity and STN calcium signals.

claim: Stimulation at 100 Hz caused an increase in STN activity (p=9.54 × 10–7) mirroring an increase in velocity (p=1.11 × 10–9).
source: The same was true for stimulation at 100 Hz, with an increase in STN activity (p=9.54 × 10–7) mirroring an increase in velocity (Figure 2E–F, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C; p=1.11 × 10–9).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that 100 Hz STN DBS increased both movement velocity and STN activity.

claim: Rather than inhibiting the STN, STN DBS increases STN activity.
source: This result suggests that, rather than inhibiting the STN, STN DBS increases STN activity.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the experimental data about the effect of STN DBS on STN activity.

claim: Levodopa increased movement velocity (p=9.69 × 10–10) and percent time moving (p=9.56 × 10–10), evoked contralesional rotations (p=1.73 × 10–6), and caused minimal dyskinesias.
source: In these animals, levodopa increased movement velocity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1L-M; p=9.69 × 10–10) and percent time moving (Figure 2—figure supplement 1N; p=9.56 × 10–10), evoked contralesional rotations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1O; p=1.73 × 10–6), and caused minimal dyskinesias (Figure 2—figure supplement 1P).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing the effects of levodopa on multiple behavioral measures.

claim: Though all mice showed improvements in movement with levodopa (p=1.66 × 10–3 for velocity, p=3.91 × 10–3 for rotation bias), changes in STN calcium were variable.
source: In these sessions, though all mice showed improvements in movement (p=1.66 × 10–3 for velocity, p=3.91 × 10–3 for rotation bias), changes in STN calcium were variable (Figure 2G–H; Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that levodopa improved movement but had variable effects on STN calcium signals.

claim: In some mice, STN activity decreased with levodopa, while in others it increased: STN activity was not significantly changed across the entire group (p=0.90).
source: In some mice, STN activity decreased, while in others it increased: STN activity was not significantly changed across the entire group (Figure 2H; p=0.90).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing variable effects of levodopa on STN activity.

claim: Injection with saline did not improve movement parameters, nor did it produce significant changes in STN activity (p=0.084).
source: Injection with saline did not improve movement parameters, nor did it produce significant changes in STN activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E-F; p=0.084).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that saline injection did not affect movement or STN activity.

claim: Levodopa caused a modest, though significant, decrease in STN firing rates (p=0.029) in parallel with its impact on movement (p=3.13 × 10–4 for velocity, p=9.77 × 10–4 for rotation bias).
source: In parallel with its impact on movement (p=3.13 × 10–4 for velocity, p=9.77 × 10–4 for rotation bias), levodopa caused a modest, though significant, decrease in STN firing rates (Figure 2I–J, Figure 2—figure supplement 2G; p=0.029).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that levodopa decreased STN firing rates and improved movement.

claim: The fact that bulk calcium signals did not reflect the modest reductions in STN firing seen with electrophysiology may relate to differential sensitivity of the two methods.
source: The fact that bulk calcium signals did not reflect the modest reductions in STN firing seen with electrophysiology may relate to differential sensitivity of the two methods.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about the reason for the discrepancy between calcium signals and electrophysiology.

claim: Despite the fact that DBS and levodopa both improve movement parameters, they appear to alter overall activity level in opposite directions.
source: Despite the fact that DBS and levodopa both improve movement parameters, they appear to alter overall activity level in opposite directions.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the experimental data comparing the effects of DBS and levodopa on neural activity.

claim: STN is believed to regulate motor function via excitatory projections to basal ganglia output nuclei.
source: Though the STN is a critical node within the basal ganglia circuit, especially in regard to dysfunction in PD and its treatment, it is believed to regulate motor function via excitatory projections to basal ganglia output nuclei.
evidence: The manuscript references established scientific knowledge about STN function.

claim: STN DBS is likely to cause changes in the activity of nearby axons, and thus may have complex downstream effects.
source: In addition, STN DBS is likely to cause changes in the activity of nearby axons, and thus may have complex downstream effects.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about the potential effects of STN DBS on nearby axons.

claim: STN DBS in mice increased movement velocity across a wide range of frequencies (p=1.33 × 10–5 for 60 Hz, p=4.99 × 10–6 for 100 Hz).
source: As before, STN DBS in these mice increased movement velocity across a wide range of frequencies (Figure 3B–E; p=1.33 × 10–5 for 60 Hz, p=4.99 × 10–6 for 100 Hz; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, Supplementary file 1, table 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that STN DBS increased movement velocity in mice with SNr recordings.

claim: STN DBS (at both 60 and 100 Hz) increased SNr activity (p=4.14 × 10–5 for 60 Hz, p=3.32 × 10–5 for 100 Hz).
source: Consistent with our results in the STN, STN DBS (at both 60 and 100 Hz) increased SNr activity (Figure 3B–E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D; p=4.14 × 10–5 for 60 Hz, p=3.32 × 10–5 for 100 Hz).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that STN DBS increased SNr activity.

claim: Contrary to the basal ganglia rate model, and the inhibition theory of DBS, both STN and SNr activities are increased by STN DBS.
source: Contrary to the basal ganglia rate model, and the inhibition theory of DBS, these findings suggest that both STN and SNr activities are increased by STN DBS.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the experimental data about the effect of STN DBS on STN and SNr activity.

claim: Levodopa increased movement velocity (p=0.016) and caused a contralesional rotation bias (p=7.81 × 10–3) in mice with SNr recordings.
source: In the same parkinsonian mice, levodopa increased movement velocity (p=0.016) and caused a contralesional rotation bias (Figure 3F–G; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E; p=7.81 × 10–3).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing the effects of levodopa on movement in mice with SNr recordings.

claim: Levodopa caused a marked decrease in SNr neural activity as measured by fiber photometry (p=6.68 × 10–6).
source: In parallel, we observed a marked decrease in SNr neural activity as measured by fiber photometry (Figure 3F–G; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E; p=6.68 × 10–6).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that levodopa decreased SNr activity.

claim: Saline neither improved movement parameters nor significantly changed SNr calcium signals (p=0.31).
source: In contrast, saline neither improved movement parameters nor significantly changed SNr calcium signals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F-G; p=0.31).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that saline injection did not affect movement or SNr activity.

claim: Single-unit electrophysiological recordings showed profound reductions in SNr firing rate (p=0.012) during therapeutic levodopa treatment.
source: Single-unit electrophysiological recordings also showed profound reductions in SNr firing rate (p=0.012) during therapeutic levodopa treatment (Figure 3H–I; Figure 3—figure supplement 1H), similar to findings in the GPi of parkinsonian NHPs (Papa et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that levodopa decreased SNr firing rate, and cites a similar finding in primates.

claim: GCaMP fiber photometry and electrophysiology revealed qualitatively similar changes in SNr activity in response to levodopa.
source: Thus, GCaMP fiber photometry and electrophysiology revealed qualitatively similar changes in SNr activity in response to levodopa, supporting the idea that these two measures of neural activity have substantial concordance.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the experimental data comparing fiber photometry and electrophysiology.

claim: These experiments show marked differences in how STN DBS and levodopa impact neural activity, suggesting that STN DBS does not exert therapeutic effects through inhibition of STN or SNr.
source: Furthermore, these experiments show marked differences in how STN DBS and levodopa impact neural activity, suggesting that STN DBS does not exert therapeutic effects through inhibition of STN or SNr.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the experimental data about the mechanism of STN DBS.

claim: A more recent theory posits that STN DBS acts through antidromic activation of the hyperdirect pathway: primary motor cortex (M1) neurons that project monosynaptically to the STN.
source: While we did not observe inhibition in either the STN or SNr during STN DBS, a more recent theory posits that STN DBS acts through antidromic activation of the hyperdirect pathway: primary motor cortex (M1) neurons that project monosynaptically to the STN.
evidence: The manuscript references a theory from prior studies about the mechanism of STN DBS.

claim: STN-projecting M1 neurons have been shown to send collaterals to the STN with parent axons in the cerebral peduncle.
source: This strategy restricted expression of GCaMP6s to STN-projecting M1 neurons, which previously have been shown to send collaterals to the STN with parent axons in the cerebral peduncle (Kita and Kita, 2012; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study showing the anatomy of STN-projecting M1 neurons.

claim: DBS increased movement velocity across a wide range of stimulation frequencies in parkinsonian mice with hyperdirect pathway recordings (p=1.51 × 10–9 for 60 Hz, p=4.14 × 10–7 for 100 Hz).
source: As in other parkinsonian mice, DBS increased movement velocity across a wide range of stimulation frequencies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, Supplementary file 1, table 2; Figure 4B–E; p=1.51 × 10–9 for 60 Hz, p=4.14 × 10–7 for 100 Hz).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that STN DBS increased movement velocity in mice with hyperdirect pathway recordings.

claim: Despite the consistent therapeutic effects of 60 Hz STN DBS, hyperdirect M1 calcium responses were surprisingly variable: some mice showed increases, while the calcium signal in other mice decreased or did not change (p=0.084).
source: Despite the consistent therapeutic effects of 60 Hz STN DBS (Figure 4C, top), hyperdirect M1 calcium responses were surprisingly variable: some mice showed increases, while the calcium signal in other mice decreased or did not change (Figure 4C, bottom; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C; p=0.084).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing variable effects of 60 Hz STN DBS on hyperdirect M1 activity.

claim: 100 Hz STN DBS increased movement velocity, and M1 activity was more consistently increased during stimulation (p=5.88 × 10–5).
source: In the same mice, 100 Hz STN DBS also increased movement velocity (Figure 4E, top), but in this case M1 activity was more consistently increased during stimulation (Figure 4E, bottom; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D; p=5.88 × 10–5).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that 100 Hz STN DBS increased both movement velocity and M1 activity.

claim: These results suggested poor correlation between hyperdirect M1 activity and the behavioral benefits of STN DBS.
source: These results suggested poor correlation between hyperdirect M1 activity and the behavioral benefits of STN DBS.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the experimental data about the relationship between M1 activity and DBS benefits.

claim: Movement velocity during DBS did not correlate with change in hyperdirect M1 neural activity (R2=−0.14, p=0.96).
source: We found that movement velocity during DBS did not correlate with change in hyperdirect M1 neural activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F; R2=−0.14, p=0.96).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing no correlation between movement velocity and M1 activity during DBS.

claim: While certain stimulation parameters may promote hyperdirect pathway activity, these changes do not strongly correlate with behavioral improvements during DBS.
source: These findings suggest that while certain stimulation parameters may promote hyperdirect pathway activity, these changes do not strongly correlate with behavioral improvements during DBS.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the experimental data about the relationship between hyperdirect pathway activity and DBS benefits.

claim: Increases in hyperdirect M1 activity evolved more slowly during STN DBS than increases in STN and SNr activity.
source: Additionally, we noted that increases in hyperdirect M1 activity evolved more slowly during STN DBS than increases in STN and SNr activity.
evidence: The manuscript presents an observation from the experimental data about the kinetics of M1 activity during DBS.

claim: The activity of neurons mediating the therapeutic effects of STN DBS would be predicted to change on a similar timescale to behavior.
source: The activity of neurons mediating the therapeutic effects of STN DBS would be predicted to change on a similar timescale to behavior.
evidence: The manuscript makes a logical prediction about the expected kinetics of neural activity mediating DBS effects.

claim: Across all STN DBS conditions, movement velocity increased with a rise time of 2.8±0.6 s after stimulation commenced.
source: Across all STN DBS conditions, movement velocity increased with a rise time of 2.8±0.6 s after stimulation commenced.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing the rise time of movement velocity during DBS.

claim: STN calcium signals during 60 or 100 Hz STN DBS lagged movement velocity by 2.6±1.1 s.
source: STN calcium signals during 60 or 100 Hz STN DBS lagged movement velocity by 2.6±1.1 s.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing the lag between STN calcium signals and movement velocity during DBS.

claim: The lag in SNr activity compared to movement velocity was 3.7±1.8 s.
source: We observed a relatively similar lag comparing SNr calcium signals to the corresponding movement velocity traces (3.7±1.8 s).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing the lag between SNr calcium signals and movement velocity during DBS.

claim: The lag in hyperdirect M1 activity was markedly longer (17.3±3.1 s).
source: However, the lag in hyperdirect M1 activity was markedly longer (17.3±3.1 s).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing the lag between M1 activity and movement velocity during DBS.

claim: These kinetics indicate STN and SNr activity evolve on a timescale similar to the movement benefits of STN DBS, while hyperdirect M1 activity, as measured by fiber photometry, evolves more slowly.
source: These kinetics indicate STN and SNr activity evolve on a timescale similar to the movement benefits of STN DBS, while hyperdirect M1 activity, as measured by fiber photometry, evolves more slowly.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the experimental data about the kinetics of neural activity during DBS.

claim: Mice with surgical removal of the ipsilesional M1 still showed a significant increase in movement velocity in response to 100 Hz STN DBS (p=8.24 × 10–3).
source: Remarkably, these mice still showed a significant increase in movement velocity in response to 100 Hz STN DBS (Figure 5B–C; p=8.24 × 10–3).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that STN DBS was still effective after M1 lesion.

claim: It is unlikely that antidromic activation of M1 is the primary driver of the therapeutic benefit of STN DBS in parkinsonian mice.
source: Thus, it is unlikely that antidromic activation of M1 is the primary driver of the therapeutic benefit of STN DBS in parkinsonian mice.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the experimental data about the role of M1 in DBS benefits.

claim: In parkinsonian mice, STN activity increases around movement initiation, consistent with the idea that STN neurons encode some aspects of movement.
source: As previously noted, in parkinsonian mice, STN activity increases around movement initiation (Figure 6A, left), consistent with the idea that STN neurons encode some aspects of movement.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing STN activity around movement initiation and draws an inference about STN function.

claim: Although the overall average calcium signal was increased during DBS, the movement-aligned increase in STN activity was abolished during therapeutic STN DBS at 100 Hz.
source: We found that although the overall average calcium signal was increased during DBS (Figure 2), the movement-aligned increase in STN activity was abolished during therapeutic STN DBS at 100 Hz (Figure 6A, right).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that DBS abolished movement-aligned STN activity.

claim: This observation suggested that STN movement encoding was disrupted by STN DBS.
source: This observation suggested that STN movement encoding was disrupted by STN DBS.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference from the experimental data about the effect of DBS on STN movement encoding.

claim: With low effect stimulation parameters, STN calcium signals increased around movement onset, as they did during baseline (no stimulation) periods.
source: With low effect stimulation parameters, STN calcium signals increased around movement onset, as they did during baseline (no stimulation) periods.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that low effect stimulation did not disrupt movement-aligned STN activity.

claim: During high effect stimulation, STN calcium signals changed minimally around movement onset, with a peak-to-trough change of <1.
source: However, during high effect stimulation, STN calcium signals changed minimally around movement onset, with a peak-to-trough change of <1 (Figure 6C).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that high effect stimulation disrupted movement-aligned STN activity.

claim: The normal movement-related increase in STN activity was strongly suppressed only during highly effective stimulation (p=1.48 × 10–11 for pre vs. high, p=0.54 for pre vs. low).
source: When comparing STN activity across all high effect vs. all low effect stimulation parameters rather than individually, the normal movement-related increase in STN activity was strongly suppressed only during highly effective stimulation (Figure 6D; p=1.48 × 10–11 for pre vs. high, p=0.54 for pre vs. low).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that only highly effective stimulation suppressed movement-related STN activity.

claim: STN DBS disrupts movement-related STN activity and this disruption is specific to behaviorally beneficial stimulation parameters.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that STN DBS disrupts movement-related STN activity and furthermore that this disruption is specific to behaviorally beneficial stimulation parameters.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the experimental data about the relationship between disruption of movement-related STN activity and DBS effectiveness.

claim: It remains critical to determine which changes in neural activity causally contribute to the therapeutic mechanism(s) of STN DBS.
source: However, it remains critical to determine which changes in neural activity causally contribute to the therapeutic mechanism(s) of STN DBS.
evidence: The manuscript states the importance of determining causal mechanisms of DBS.

claim: STN neurons showed both excitatory and inhibitory responses to optical stimulation, as has been observed previously in anesthetized STN recordings in rats.
source: As has been observed previously in anesthetized STN recordings in rats (Yu et al., 2020), STN neurons showed both excitatory and inhibitory responses to optical stimulation (Figure 7B–E; Figure 7—figure supplement 1B-C).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing variable responses of STN neurons to optical stimulation and cites a similar finding in rats.

claim: Both constant and 50 Hz optical stimulation paradigms caused similar decreases in overall firing rate (p=0.98 comparing relative firing rates during constant and 50 Hz stimulation).
source: However, both stimulation paradigms caused similar decreases in overall firing rate (Figure 7C and E; p=0.98 comparing relative firing rates during constant and 50 Hz stimulation, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that both optical stimulation paradigms decreased STN firing rate.

claim: The response of STN neurons to optical stimulation differed between in vivo/freely moving and ex vivo preparations.
source: Of note, the response of STN neurons to optical stimulation differed between in vivo/freely moving and ex vivo preparations.

claim: Many therapeutic approaches to PD have been predicated on the idea that inhibition of hyperactive basal ganglia nuclei is required for therapeutic benefit.
source: Many therapeutic approaches to PD have been predicated on the idea that inhibition of hyperactive basal ganglia nuclei is required for therapeutic benefit, but our findings, as well as recent work using closed-loop DBS (Bouthour et al., 2019; Johnson et al., 2016; Rosin et al., 2011) indicate non-rate-based alterations in activity can improve movement.
